The paper reviews prior efforts to integrate human factors with infrastructure resilience analysis, identifies where those efforts fall short at the operational layer, and sets out five research priorities: measurement that is feasible at operational scale; data practices that turn existing records into modeling-ready inputs; hybrid modeling that combines agent-based, system dynamics, and network methods; cross-scale and cross-domain integration that does not overstate transferability; and governance that protects both data quality and the people who generate it. This commentary, authored by Fellows of the Young Academy of Europe (FYAE), outlines how this governance framework is reshaping international chemical collaboration, emphasizing the urgent need for updated research security practices, the emergence of the role of Security-Safety Liaison as a practical bridge between laboratory safety, regulatory compliance, and security-sensitive research governance, and the importance of harmonized safety standards to protect European interests in an era of intensified geostrategic competition. Their argument is that the framework marks a shift in how research and innovation are understood, from soft power towards strategic assets serving European resilience, competitiveness and sovereignty. They draw out practical consequences for international chemical collaboration, including updated research security practice and harmonised safety standards. Their central proposal is a security-safety liaison role bridging laboratory safety, regulatory compliance and security-sensitive research governance. This embodies what they describe as a move from safety as internal risk management towards safety as part of a wider architecture of strategic resilience and technological sovereignty.

strand_a.title: EU–China research cooperation under a “de-risking” framework: the securitisation of knowledge in EU science policy (2021–2025)
strand_a.summary: EU–China research cooperation under a “de-risking” framework: the securitisation of knowledge in EU science policy (2021–2025). The article contributes to debates on geoeconomics and science diplomacy by specifying how de-risking is institutionalised in research governance, and by highlighting narrative contestation as a constitutive element of knowledge securitisation. Drawing on securitisation theory and a qualitative analysis of publicly available EU policy documents—including the Horizon Europe regulation and participation rules (Articles 22(5)– (6)), the European Economic Security Strategy, and the 2024 Council Recommendation on enhancing research security—alongside Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) readouts and state-media commentaries, the article traces how “research security” is constructed and operationalised.

strand_a.reader_why: Shows inequality reproduced through everyday practice, not just funding and governance structures.
strand_a.reader_more: This study traces how knowledge is made in five sub-Saharan African and West European forest sustainability collaborations, using positioning analysis of meetings and fieldwork supplemented by interviews. The finding is that European collaborators disproportionately shaped approaches while African collaborators adapted to European practices, with European approaches operating as the default mode. African approaches were taken up where supporting conditions existed, notably fieldwork expertise and disproportionate persistence by those proposing them. African collaborators shaped practice outside meeting spaces in less visible ways and faced barriers to equal participation arising from sociocultural and material factors, with African women encountering combined gender and geography disadvantages. The author frames this as showing how routine daily processes both reproduce and can counter power asymmetries.

deep_analysis.research_question: How asymmetries of epistemic authority emerge in the everyday practices of African-European research collaborations.
deep_analysis.main_finding: European approaches functioned as the default in all five collaborations, with African partners adapting and needing exceptional persistence or specific fieldwork expertise for their approaches to be adopted, and African women facing compounded barriers.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Positioning analysis of meetings and fieldwork across five forest sustainability collaborations, complemented by interviews.
deep_analysis.qualification: Five collaborations in one research field, observed qualitatively; findings describe mechanisms rather than establishing how widespread the pattern is.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Bears on the quality and equity of European international research partnerships, a stated aim of EU global cooperation policy.

strand_a.title: Data scraping for AI model training and data privacy: a comparative analysis of United States and European Union Data Privacy Laws
strand_a.authors: Olumide Timothy Ajayi, Chukwuemezie Charles Emejuo, Francis Aondongu Wayo, Samuel Esezoobo
strand_a.summary: Data scraping for AI model training and data privacy: a comparative analysis of United States and European Union Data Privacy Laws. In this note, the authors explore the intersection between AI model training and data scraping using a doctrinal research method, further interrogating the lawfulness of scraping under extant data privacy laws in the United States (U.S.) and the European Union (EU). On the other hand, data scraping of publicly available personal data violates the EU data protection laws, unless it satisfies the lawful basis requirements of Article 6 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
strand_a.core_message: Abstract AI (AI) has made data not only the choicest but also a very susceptible commodity.

strand_a.reader_title: Why EU privacy law makes scraping data for AI training far harder than US law
strand_a.reader_what: Scraping public personal data is broadly permissible in the US but rarely justifiable under the GDPR.
strand_a.reader_why: The gap shapes where firms can lawfully source training data for AI models.
strand_a.reader_more: The authors compare how United States and European Union privacy rules treat the mass collection of web data used to train AI models. They conclude that in the US the decisive question is whether the data was publicly accessible, while in the EU public availability is not enough on its own. Under the GDPR a scraper still needs a lawful basis under Article 6, which the authors think will almost never be satisfied in practice. They also observe that national data protection authorities have enforced this unevenly, so the practical position differs between member states. They argue privacy law should be reformed to reconcile the two aims rather than left as it stands.

deep_analysis.research_question: Whether scraping data to train AI models is lawful under US and EU data privacy law.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Public accessibility largely legitimises scraping in the US, whereas the GDPR's lawful-basis test makes scraping of personal data very hard to justify in the EU, though enforcement varies by member state.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Doctrinal legal analysis comparing existing US and EU privacy instruments, centred on GDPR Article 6.
deep_analysis.qualification: A doctrinal reading of the law rather than empirical evidence about scraping practice or enforcement outcomes; the reform proposal is the authors' own recommendation.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Directly concerns the legal conditions under which European AI developers can assemble training data.

strand_a.summary: Can science diplomacy help safeguard science as a global public good? Abstract In a world where geopolitical tensions strongly impinge on international scientific collaboration and where some scientific information has significant commercial value, the notion of science and practice of it as a global public good are under pressure and so are the ways to pursue it. Science diplomacy acknowledges that science impacts diplomacy and diplomacy impacts science, and that both cooperation and competition shape the diverse practices of science diplomacy: from science fostering international relations and serving global public goods to foreign and security policy interests conflicting with the notion of science as an open collaborative enterprise.

strand_a.reader_why: Convergence tests indicate narrowing cross-country disparities in AI diffusion across the EU.
strand_a.reader_more: This paper examines what determines AI adoption among manufacturing and service enterprises across the 27 EU member states, using a balanced panel combining Eurostat's enterprise ICT usage survey, the Digital Intensity Index and the Community Innovation Survey across two waves in 2023 and 2025. Digital infrastructure emerges as the strongest predictor, with the Digital Intensity Index showing a significant positive effect across pooled, random-effects and fixed-effects specifications. Large firms consistently report higher adoption than smaller ones. Central and Eastern European countries still lag Western Europe but record the fastest growth, with Romania showing a 223 percent increase. Tests of sigma and beta convergence indicate narrowing disparities, which the author reads as a catching-up process in AI diffusion across the Union.

deep_analysis.research_question: What determines AI adoption among EU enterprises, and whether cross-country disparities in adoption are narrowing.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Digital intensity is the strongest and most robust predictor of AI adoption, large firms adopt more than smaller ones, and convergence tests indicate Central and Eastern European states are catching up fastest despite remaining behind.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Balanced panel of 27 member states across 2023 and 2025 survey waves, combining three Eurostat-based datasets, estimated with pooled OLS, random-effects and fixed-effects models.
deep_analysis.qualification: Only two survey waves, so convergence inference rests on a short series; percentage growth figures such as Romania's are large partly because the starting base is low.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Measures whether AI capability is spreading across the Union or concentrating, with direct implications for cohesion and industrial policy.

strand_a.reader_title: EU battery projects converge on some environmental assessment choices but not the decisive ones
strand_a.reader_what: Five Horizon Europe projects agree on functional units and databases but diverge on system boundaries.
strand_a.reader_why: Divergent recycling and electricity assumptions make project results incomparable for benchmarking and policy.
strand_a.reader_more: Life cycle assessment estimates a product's environmental burden across its whole life and is widely used in EU-funded battery research. This paper, from the Battery Heroes sustainability working group, reviews how five Horizon Europe battery projects actually apply it. It finds emerging convergence on several choices: capacity-based functional units of one kilowatt-hour, reliance on ecoinvent databases, and growing adoption of the Environmental Footprint 3.1 method. Substantial variability persists in system boundary definitions, end-of-life and recycling modelling, electricity assumptions and reporting practice, all of which can materially change results. The authors propose a minimum harmonised reporting set to improve comparability and support alignment with the Product Environmental Footprint method and the EU Battery Regulation.

strand_a.reader_what: Argues China's institutional setup lets domestic imbalance reinforce external industrial competitiveness, shown through electric vehicles.

strand_a.reader_more: This article examines China's Dual Circulation Strategy, introduced to rebalance the economy toward domestic demand while protecting external competitiveness. The authors note a paradox: household consumption has not risen as intended, yet external industrial expansion has intensified. They argue the strategy consolidates rather than breaks with the party-led development model, and that under this institutional configuration domestic weakness can actively reinforce external competitiveness. Using electric vehicles as their case, they trace how persistent investment bias, industrial scaling and control over critical inputs strengthened China's position in global value chains. They draw an explicit contrast with the European Union, where internal structural constraints tend to erode external competitiveness instead.

strand_a.summary: AI adoption as technology transfer: an integrative review and conceptual framework for governance, validation and knowledge preservation. Drawing on principles established in regulated industries; pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, aerospace and advanced manufacturing; it proposes that successful AI implementation depends on the same characteristics that define successful technology transfer: reproducibility, robustness and validation; traceability and knowledge preservation; and process control and continuous verification. strand_a.reader_title: Italian doctoral students prefer to stay, even at a salary or career penalty
strand_a.reader_what: PhD students prefer remaining in Italy despite poor pay and scarce vacancies; salary is not decisive.
strand_a.reader_why: Retention policy built mainly around salary may be aimed at the wrong lever.
strand_a.reader_more: This study uses a discrete choice experiment, in which respondents repeatedly choose between hypothetical job offers, to identify what would keep doctoral students in Italy rather than pushing them abroad. The result runs against the usual expectation. Despite job insecurity, internationally uncompetitive salaries, scarce vacancies and a constrained national labour market, these students, including strong research performers, still prefer to stay. They are reluctant to migrate even when offered non-research jobs lacking autonomy and long-term stability, and salary alone is not the primary determinant of migration decisions. Staying is often experienced as accepting a salary or career penalty in order to continue research in their current country or city.

deep_analysis.research_question: Which job conditions talent-producing countries can adopt to reduce brain drain among doctoral graduates.
deep_analysis.main_finding: PhD students in Italy, including high research performers, prefer to remain despite adverse conditions; salary alone is not the primary determinant of migration decisions, and staying is often framed as accepting a salary or career penalty to continue research.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Discrete choice experiment eliciting stated preferences over hypothetical job offers from PhD students in Italy.
deep_analysis.qualification: Stated preferences over hypothetical offers may diverge from actual migration behaviour; one country and one career stage, and the finding concerns willingness to stay rather than availability of suitable positions.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Bears directly on European retention of doctoral research talent and on which policy levers would work.

strand_a.reader_title: Once income is controlled for, AI adoption no longer predicts EU labour productivity
strand_a.reader_what: After controlling for economic development, only GDP per capita significantly predicted labour productivity.
strand_a.reader_why: Indicates digital technology alone does not deliver productivity gains without complementary economic capability.
strand_a.reader_more: This study relates enterprise AI adoption and workforce digital skills to labour productivity across the 27 EU member states, using Eurostat and OECD data in a cross-sectional design. Simple pairwise correlations look encouraging, with productivity positively associated with AI adoption, digital skills and GDP per capita alike. The regression tells a different story: once economic development is controlled for, GDP per capita is the only statistically significant predictor, and the independent effects of AI adoption and digital skills cease to be significant. The authors read this as evidence that digital technologies do not by themselves guarantee productivity gains. Their argument is that complementary economic capabilities are what translate digital transformation into measurable output.

deep_analysis.research_question: How enterprise AI adoption and workforce digital skills relate to labour productivity across EU member states.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Positive bivariate associations for AI adoption and digital skills disappear once economic development is controlled for, leaving GDP per capita as the only statistically significant predictor of labour productivity.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Cross-sectional analysis of Eurostat and OECD data for 27 EU member states using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and ordinary least squares regression.
deep_analysis.qualification: A single cross-section of 27 country-level observations, a small sample with high collinearity between wealth, skills and adoption; a non-significant coefficient here is weak evidence of no effect rather than proof of none.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Directly tests whether AI diffusion is translating into European productivity gains, and finds country-level evidence does not support it.

strand_a.reader_more: This issue brief examines whether the United States has the workforce to staff the front-end semiconductor fabrication capacity it is trying to rebuild. strand_a.reader_more: The article analyses how the adopted EU Artificial Intelligence Act distributes obligations along the AI value chain, focusing on general-purpose or foundation models. It proposes a taxonomy of foundation model providers, fine-tuners, integrators and deployers, and examines the interfaces between them, including model and system documentation and logging. Using principles of control, foreseeability, benefit and capability, it argues that those who design and train foundation models should carry upstream transparency and safety duties, while those adapting or deploying systems carry downstream risk management and oversight. strand_a.reader_title: Study maps ten bottlenecks holding back Europe digital single market
strand_a.reader_what: Report identifies ten cross-border bottlenecks clustering into four structural dysfunctions and proposes four strategic priorities.
strand_a.reader_why: Frames digital market fragmentation as a direct constraint on European strategic autonomy.
strand_a.reader_more: This Sitra study, prepared with the Centre for European Policy Studies and Professor Paul Timmers, examines structural obstacles to the digital single market. It reviews Commission, business and think tank work from 2023 to 2026, identifies ten bottlenecks that consistently limit companies ability to operate and scale across borders, and uses systems mapping to show how they reinforce one another. The bottlenecks cluster into four dysfunctions: fragmented and unevenly implemented regulation, digital infrastructure confined within national silos, skills and labour mobility lagging behind digital transformation, and a financing and innovation ecosystem that does not support European digital companies scaling globally. From these the authors derive four strategic priorities: use digital, control digital, policy leadership, and simplify digital.

deep_analysis.main_finding: Ten reinforcing bottlenecks cluster into four structural dysfunctions, and the authors argue fragmentation now limits not just the economy but Europe ability to shape global digital rules.

deep_analysis.qualification: Synthesis of existing studies and expert input rather than new empirical measurement; priorities are proposals.

strand_a.reader_title: Four scenarios for Europe's growth model in an age of strategic capitalism
strand_a.reader_what: Paper argues the EU's growth model relies on externally sourced inputs and technologies, leaving it structurally fragile.
strand_a.reader_why: Only one of four scenarios, Strategic Europe, aligns competitiveness, control and innovation direction.
strand_a.reader_more: Strategic capitalism here describes an environment in which industrial policy, investment screening and export controls have become ordinary instruments of statecraft. The authors argue that Europe's current model, built on externally sourced inputs, technologies and infrastructures, is fragile under those conditions, and that its innovation future depends on aligning competitiveness with control over critical economic flows and a clear direction for innovation. They set out four trajectories: Dependent Europe, innovation without control or direction; Fortress Europe, control without dynamism; Fragmented Europe, ambition without alignment; and Strategic Europe, which aligns all three and is the only one they see leading to sustained technological leadership. The scenarios are analytical constructions used to structure the argument rather than predictions.

deep_analysis.research_question: What growth model does the EU need for innovation-led competitiveness under conditions of strategic capitalism?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The EU's reliance on externally sourced inputs, technologies and infrastructures makes its growth model structurally fragile; of four constructed trajectories only Strategic Europe aligns competitiveness, control over critical flows and innovation direction, which the authors argue requires stronger national and EU policy alignment.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual and scenario-based policy analysis situated in geoeconomics literature; report PDF supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Scenario-based argument rather than empirical modelling, so the trajectories illustrate possibilities and are not forecasts. Note that the package's scanner metadata names a different author; the paper itself is by Mikael Wigell and Sinikukka Saari.

strand_a.reader_title: Finnish research funder's policy on security risks in international collaboration
strand_a.reader_what: Finnish law obliges the funder to address research security while preserving researchers' freedom to choose topics.
strand_a.reader_why: Shows how a funder reconciles security screening with academic freedom in statute.
strand_a.reader_more: This page sets out the Research Council of Finland's overall position on research security, distinct from its detailed application guidance. The council states it is obliged by law to ensure research security risks are addressed in funded projects, collaborations and the use of results, while the same law specifies that security considerations must not restrict a researcher's choice of topic or methods. It defines research security as anticipating and managing risks in international collaboration, and identifies three categories: transfer of critical knowledge and technology enabling military or intelligence use, harmful interference such as disinformation or induced self-censorship, and uses undermining fundamental rights or European values. Responsibility for the assessment rests with the applicant.

deep_analysis.main_finding: Finnish law requires the national research funder to address research security across funded projects and its own international cooperation, while explicitly barring security considerations from restricting researchers' choice of topic or method.

strand_a.reader_more: This study evaluates long-term prospects for sustainable agricultural productivity growth under different assumptions about public agricultural research spending, treating that spending as the key productivity driver. It also asks what happens if research focus shifts from maximising yield towards technologies that save inputs such as fertilisers and pesticides. Using the MAGNET computable general equilibrium model, the projections identify China, India and Brazil as regions gaining high productivity growth from agricultural research, while Sub-Saharan Africa struggles with low growth and substantially rising greenhouse gas emissions. Overall emissions are projected to grow faster than agricultural output. The authors find sustainable growth becomes feasible if high-income countries reorient research programmes, with chemical input use falling by as much as 30 percent and limited effect on food prices.

strand_a.reader_what: Builds a gap indicator showing wide and diverging differences in how countries convert research spending into output.
strand_a.reader_why: Suggests raising research spending alone will not close innovation gaps between member states.
strand_a.reader_more: This paper studies the relationship between research and development spending and innovation output across the 27 EU member states from 2011 to 2024. Innovation output is measured two ways, through patent activity and high-technology exports. Using a correlated random effects panel model, the authors take the unexplained residual and turn it into a transformation gap indicator: how far a country's actual innovation output sits above or below what its research spending and structural conditions would predict. They report substantial variation between countries and distinct trajectories over time, with some countries converging on their expected performance while others drift further from it. The contribution is combining a static picture with how these gaps evolve.

deep_analysis.main_finding: Transformation gaps vary substantially across EU countries and follow divergent paths over time, with some converging towards expected performance and others showing widening deviations.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Panel data for 27 EU countries, 2011 to 2024, using a correlated random effects model with patent activity and high-tech exports as outputs, and model residuals as the gap indicator.
deep_analysis.qualification: The gap indicator is a model residual, so it reflects whatever the model omits as well as genuine efficiency differences; patents and high-tech exports are partial proxies for innovation.

strand_a.reader_more: The sample covers 231 leading corporate research spenders with inventive activity spread across 118 European regions between 2000 and 2018. strand_a.reader_what: Exposure and worker use are widespread, while invention and firm adoption stay concentrated in wealthy, high-skill hubs.

strand_a.reader_more: The study uses six indicators across EU NUTS-2 regions, the statistical unit roughly equivalent to a province or large region, to separate three distinct things: where AI is invented, where workers and industries are exposed to it, and where it is actually used. The pattern the authors call a spatial paradox is that exposure and individual use spread fairly broadly while invention and firm-level adoption cluster in regions with high income and highly educated workforces. Income and human capital track AI activity closely, while trade openness runs the other way. These are associations across regions, not causal estimates.

strand_a.reader_more: The Fifth Freedom here means free and equal movement of researchers, open access to scientific knowledge, and research funding circulating across the EU. Sixty-two researchers in eleven member states answered three open questions and one closed one, and about 89 per cent backed formal EU recognition of the freedom. Administrative barriers and discriminatory hiring or funding eligibility were each raised by roughly 48 per cent of respondents, with non-recognition of qualifications next at 33 per cent and named as the most-demanded reform. Respondents supplied costed personal cases, including sworn translation fees of two to three hundred euros per diploma and foreign experience counted at half value in salary scales. The authors describe the sample as a self-selected pilot, not statistically representative.

strand_a.reader_title: Germany has Europe's largest AI workforce but distributes it unevenly
strand_a.reader_what: Analysis of 117,000 profiles finds AI talent split between southern industry and startup-heavy Berlin and Hamburg.
strand_a.reader_why: Attracting, retaining and directing AI talent are three separate problems needing different policies.
strand_a.reader_more: This data brief maps Germany's AI workforce of roughly 117,000 people, about double Italy's, across sixteen states and many industries. It finds a tension between scale and concentration: Berlin has the densest AI workforce relative to population, while Bavaria and Baden-Wurttemberg hold the largest absolute numbers. Internationally trained professionals tend to enter through startups in cities like Berlin and Hamburg rather than the southern industrial firms, so policies to attract foreign researchers are distinct from building pipelines into legacy industry. Talent broadly tracks the federal AI strategy's priority sectors, with strong representation in manufacturing and robotics, but healthcare is a marked exception at roughly 3,500 professionals, about three percent of the total.

strand_a.reader_title: Collaboration and funding are both associated with less novel research, not more
strand_a.reader_what: Across European regions, scientific collaboration and research funding both correlate negatively with novelty.
strand_a.reader_why: Challenges the assumption that collaborative funded research automatically produces more original work.
strand_a.reader_more: This study uses Web of Science publication data from European regions between 2008 and 2017 to test how collaboration and funding relate to the novelty of research, measuring collaboration at five levels from country through three regional tiers to institutions, and measuring novelty through keyword combinations. The headline results run against common assumptions: there is a negative and significant relationship between scientific collaboration and novelty, and funded papers show lower novelty than unfunded ones. Funding does, however, have a significant moderating effect on the relationship between collaboration and novelty. The authors position the contribution as linking multiple levels of collaboration and funding source to novelty within bibliometric research.

strand_a.summary: FAIR-Compute: A Roadmap for Fair and Efficient Allocation of Federated Digital Research Infrastructure. FAIR-Compute studies allocation in a federated Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI) as a problem at the intersection of algorithmic game theory, transport economics and HPC scheduling. The project combined three strands of evidence: a landscape review of UK and international allocation practice (including EuroHPC, WLCG, ACCESS, JASMIN and DiRAC) supported by a stakeholder survey; a mechanism-design model of allocation under strategic and uncertain user reports; and a simulation study built on the public Fresco/Anvil workload trace and controlled synthetic stress tests.

strand_a.reader_title: Compute allocation records measure reservation, not useful work done
strand_a.reader_what: Allocation records capture occupancy rather than utilisation, so productive value cannot currently be assessed.
strand_a.reader_why: Unmanaged federation can concentrate load and harm on receiving systems while lowering average delay.
strand_a.reader_more: This preprint studies how scarce computing is allocated across federated digital research infrastructure, combining a landscape review of UK and international practice including EuroHPC, a mechanism-design model of allocation under strategic user reports, and simulation on a public workload trace. Three findings recur. First, allocation records measure occupancy, meaning resources reserved, rather than utilisation, meaning useful work done, so funders cannot currently answer whether resources deliver productive value. Second, simple transparent scheduling heuristics perform close to a full-information benchmark once tuned, so the near-term opportunity is instrumenting existing schedulers rather than replacing them. Third, unmanaged federation behaves like uncoordinated routing, minimising average delay while concentrating load on receiving systems, analogous to Braess's paradox in road networks.

strand_a.reader_more: This study compares extractive governance across five settings: lithium in Australia, cobalt in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, nickel in Canada, copper in Chile, and the European Union under the Critical Raw Materials Act. strand_a.reader_why: Peripheral universities act as anchor institutions, a role that patent and spin-off counts miss.
strand_a.reader_more: This study examines 301 universities across the European Economic Area, relating innovation outputs such as Horizon 2020 participation, patents and spin-offs, together with sustainability profiles, to regional economic and labour market outcomes. Regional scientific and human capital is strongly associated with regional GDP and employment, but technological innovation outputs show no direct conversion into growth at aggregate level, which the authors call a regional innovation paradox. Environmental sustainability performance is positively linked to innovation capacity, while social sustainability outcomes appear structurally decoupled in the short run. A multi-group analysis reveals the spatial asymmetry behind the aggregate result: returns concentrate in high-density metropolitan hubs with strong absorptive capacity, whereas in low-density peripheral regions universities function primarily as anchor institutions stabilising local economies.

strand_a.reader_more: The study examines education and training regulatory or sector bodies in Malawi technical and vocational education system, asking whether they can act as intermediaries between policy, industry and training institutions. It draws on a qualitative multi-case institutional assessment of eight such bodies, carried out under the EU-funded Zantchito Skills for Jobs Project, and applies open innovation systems theory. The stated contribution is to scholarship on innovation ecosystems, skills governance and public-private partnerships, with policy lessons for African vocational education reform.

strand_a.reader_title: Who non-academic university staff are matters more than how many there are
strand_a.reader_what: Across 401 European universities, the share of non-academic staff showed no significant efficiency effect; their composition did.
strand_a.reader_why: Challenges administrative headcount as a performance lever in European university funding and governance debates.
strand_a.reader_more: The study addresses a long-running ambiguity: administrative and technical staff may either free up academics or add bureaucratic burden. Using a sample of 401 European universities, the authors treat the heterogeneity of non-academic staff as an unobserved factor, estimate it with a nonparametric approach, and then test its effect on performance. The proportion of non-academic staff has no statistically significant effect on efficiency. The latent heterogeneity factor, capturing qualitative and structural differences beyond size and composition, significantly influences both the efficient frontier and the distribution of inefficiency. Universities combining very high staff heterogeneity with large administrative shares tend to be less efficient, a pattern the authors read as bureaucratic overload.

deep_analysis.research_question: Does the size and heterogeneity of non-academic staff affect the performance of European universities?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Non-academic staff share does not significantly affect efficiency, but their unobserved heterogeneity does, with overload effects at high levels.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Nonparametric estimation of a latent staff heterogeneity factor across 401 European universities
deep_analysis.qualification: The key variable is a latent estimated factor rather than a directly observed one, so interpretation depends on the modelling choices.

strand_a.reader_title: Removing personal identifiers made AI staff evaluations more consistent in a synthetic test
strand_a.reader_what: Stripping identifying attributes kept scores consistent while reducing variation linked to candidate identity.
strand_a.reader_why: Gives technical support to the data minimisation principle already required under EU law.
strand_a.reader_more: This proof-of-concept study tests whether removing personal identifiers from human resources data changes how large language models evaluate employees, using self-hosted open models as a security layer and a synthetic dataset. Two experiments covered automated redaction of identifying information and the effect of pseudonymisation on model-generated promotion suitability scores. Removing protected attributes preserved overall consistency of scores while reducing identity-linked variation. Most evaluations, 88 percent, were unaffected by identifier visibility, but 12 percent shifted, and Bayesian modelling identified geographic region as the strongest factor linked to that variation, with some non-European profiles scoring lower in certain conditions. The authors stress these are exploratory results needing validation on real data.

deep_analysis.qualification: The authors state clearly that this is exploratory evidence on synthetic data requiring validation on real enterprise datasets, not a definitive empirical conclusion; the on-premise architecture recommendation follows from their setup rather than a comparison of alternatives.

strand_a.reader_more: The authors use panel data covering 61 countries from 2002 to 2024 to test whether green technology innovation is associated with stronger energy security. strand_a.reader_title: Cohesion Policy transfers show no robust effect on development traps, but research spending does
strand_a.reader_what: Transfers did not robustly reduce regional entrapment risk, while higher research spending consistently did.
strand_a.reader_why: Suggests current allocation may underserve the low research-intensity regions most at risk.
strand_a.reader_more: This paper tests whether European Cohesion Policy fiscal transfers reduce the risk that EU regions fall into a development trap, meaning prolonged stagnation relative to peers. It uses a regression discontinuity design with heterogeneous treatment effects over 2000 to 2020, exploiting eligibility thresholds to approximate a causal comparison. The results do not robustly confirm a direct role for the transfers in reducing entrapment risk. Regions with higher research and development spending, however, consistently show reduced risk, which the author reads as evidence that such spending sustains long-term productivity and growth. The conclusion drawn is that the current fund allocation strategy may inadequately support regions with low research intensity and should be reassessed.

deep_analysis.research_question: Whether Cohesion Policy transfers reduce EU regions' risk of a development trap, and what role research intensity plays.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Cohesion Policy transfers show no robust direct effect on regional entrapment risk between 2000 and 2020, while higher R&D intensity is consistently associated with reduced risk.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Regression discontinuity design with heterogeneous treatment effects on EU regional data, 2000 to 2020.
deep_analysis.qualification: A null result on the direct transfer effect is not proof of no effect; the R&D result is an association within the same design, not an established causal channel. Based on the abstract.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Tests whether the EU's main regional funding instrument works, and points to research intensity as the operative factor instead.

strand_a.reader_what: Survey across 28 research fields finds reasoning language model adoption concentrated in hard sciences, widening productivity gaps.
strand_a.reader_more: The paper surveys adoption of reasoning language models, meaning AI systems designed for multi-step inference, across 28 scientific disciplines using the European Research Council classification covering social sciences and humanities, physical sciences and engineering, and life sciences. The authors argue that impact is concentrated in hard science fields and that slow adoption elsewhere is widening a gap in research productivity. They examine how these models are developed, evaluated and applied by discipline, and introduce a maturity assessment framework based on the domain-specific development and evaluation resources available. strand_a.title: Building Resilient and Robust Clean Energy Supply Chains: Challenges and Opportunities for a Sustainable Energy Transition
strand_a.summary: This report synthesizes the proceedings and key findings of the workshop "Building Resilient and Robust Clean Energy Supply Chains: Challenges and Opportunities for a Sustainable Energy Transition," co-organized by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) and the International Energy Agency's Expert Group on R&D Priority Setting and Evaluation (IEA-EGRD) on November 27-28, 2025, in Petten, The Netherlands. The discussions were structured around three core themes: navigating the overarching challenges and geopolitical shifts in supply chains; establishing effective strategies for data collection, management, and sharing; and deploying advanced modelling techniques to map supply chains. To build genuine resilience, stakeholders must move beyond static reporting by embracing near real-time monitoring, prioritizing innovations that reduce reliance on critical raw materials, and fostering continuous international collaboration to ensure a secure and equitable global energy transition.

strand_a.reader_title: Workshop report on making clean energy supply chains resilient enough to monitor
strand_a.reader_what: Experts conclude resilience requires near real-time supply chain monitoring rather than static periodic reporting.
strand_a.reader_why: Clean technology manufacturing networks now restructure geographically within a single year.
strand_a.reader_more: This report synthesises a November 2025 workshop in Petten co-organised by the Commission's Joint Research Centre and the International Energy Agency's expert group on research priority setting. Discussions covered geopolitical shifts in supply chains, data collection and sharing, and supply chain modelling. The central conclusion was that granular, high-quality data is a precondition for evidence-based policy, obstructed at present by data fragmentation, commercial opacity and component complexity. Proposed methods include using AI to extract unstructured corporate data, satellite imagery to track facility construction, and international certificates to map component origins. Participants also emphasised life cycle assessment to surface hidden environmental and social burdens, and noted that manufacturing networks restructure geographically within a year in response to tariffs, subsidies and state intervention.

deep_analysis.research_question: How clean energy supply chain vulnerabilities can be measured and reduced in highly concentrated technology markets.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Participants converged on the view that static reporting is inadequate and that resilience requires near real-time monitoring, innovation reducing critical raw material dependence, and sustained international collaboration.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Synthesis of expert discussion among policymakers, industry and researchers at a two-day workshop, rather than original data analysis.
deep_analysis.qualification: Reports a consensus reached in discussion, not tested evidence; the monitoring methods described are proposals whose feasibility and cost are not assessed here.

strand_b.reader_title: The same foresight methods do different institutional work in different governance systems

strand_b.reader_why: Covers ESPAS, the Strategic Foresight Reports, the Better Regulation Toolbox and Open Strategic Autonomy.
strand_b.reader_more: The argument is that a method is never institutionally neutral: the same scenario or expert exercise does different work depending on the governance setting it sits in. The authors distinguish technocratic, market-managerial, networked and anticipatory logics, and map functions onto each, from expert prioritisation in the first to strategic positioning in the second, stakeholder alignment and legitimacy in the third, and early warning and policy adaptation in the fourth. The EU is the focal case, with Japan and South Korea used as deliberate contrasts rather than as a symmetrical comparison. Evidence comes from bibliometric mapping of Scopus, semantic analysis of method terms and manual validation of 68 publications, so the study characterises how foresight is positioned rather than measuring its influence on decisions.

strand_b.reader_what: Eight-role agent system converts patent filings into structured intelligence reports with market evidence.
strand_b.reader_why: Separates generating and evaluating models so no system judges its own output.
strand_b.reader_more: This paper presents an eight-role multi-agent system that turns disclosed patent filings plus a free-text intelligence request into a structured competitive intelligence report. The system treats patents as seed signals, searches the open web for corresponding market evidence such as products, vendors, deployments and partnerships, and reports honestly when no evidence is found. Six frontier models execute the generative roles in parallel, while an independent pool of different models operates verifier, telemetry and judge roles, preserving the principle that the model evaluating an output is never the one that produced it. Evaluation covers four heterogeneous patent filings, reporting per-model precision, recall, semantic alignment and calibration error alongside cost and elapsed time.

strand_b.reader_title: Borrowing from deliberative democracy and philosophy of science to give foresight epistemic standing
strand_b.reader_what: Article argues reason-giving deliberation and perspectival realism can ground foresight's authority alongside established scientific disciplines.
strand_b.reader_why: Addresses why foresight struggles for epistemic authority when set against established disciplines in policymaking.
strand_b.reader_more: Perspectival realism is a position in philosophy of science holding that knowledge advances through interaction between distinct epistemic communities, each working with its own models. The author borrows it to argue that foresight produces what he calls modal models, structured accounts of what is possible, which can legitimately sit alongside other forms of evidence in policy. From deliberative democracy he takes the emphasis on pluralism and on giving reasons, presenting this as what lends foresight depth in public debate rather than merely generating options. The paper is a theoretical contribution: it offers a justification for foresight's standing in the policy process rather than evidence that adopting this framing changes practice.

deep_analysis.research_question: How can foresight establish epistemic authority in public policy alongside the natural and social sciences?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Deliberative democracy supplies an account of how reason-giving adds epistemic depth to foresight, while perspectival realism recasts foresight's outputs as modal models produced by an epistemic community, together offering a basis for foresight's standing in evidence-based policymaking.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual argument drawing on political theory and philosophy of science; publisher open-access full text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Theoretical and normative; no empirical test of whether this framing improves foresight's uptake or influence in policy processes.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns the credibility of foresight as an input to public policy, a standing question for institutionalised foresight, though not EU-specific.

strand_b.reader_title: Using functional analysis and text mining to identify emerging technologies
strand_b.reader_what: Paper proposes analysing what a technology does, rather than what it is called, to detect emerging technologies.
strand_b.reader_why: Authors argue the approach makes technology foresight affordable for small and medium-sized firms.
strand_b.reader_more: Functional analysis asks what function an artefact performs for a user, instead of describing it by its components or its label. The authors apply that lens to technology foresight, combining it with natural language processing tuned for patent documents and with expert domain knowledge. They use it to look for development patterns, spot missing elements and potential failure points, and to strengthen conventional bibliometric approaches such as S-curve analysis. Their affordability argument rests on patent and publication data being cheap and widely available, so the constraint is analytical capacity rather than access. This is a 2016 methodological proposal demonstrated by its own authors, and the text-mining techniques available have changed substantially since.

strand_b.reader_title: Method for finding policies that stay reliable when the data is too thin to model precisely
strand_b.reader_what: Proposes shifting from most probable outcomes to policies that remain robust across wide uncertainty ranges.
strand_b.reader_why: Argues conventional uncertainty analysis overstates knowledge when empirical evidence is scarce.
strand_b.reader_more: This study proposes a framework for evaluating policy in material flow analysis under deep uncertainty, motivated by the observation that conventional uncertainty methods can overstate available knowledge when data is scarce, characterising uncertainty beyond what the evidence supports. The proposed shift is away from identifying the most probable outcomes and towards identifying policies that remain reliable despite uncertainty, achieved by integrating material flow analysis with exploratory modelling that spans broad plausible ranges including extreme scenarios and assesses performance across multiple robustness metrics. The paper also offers technical solutions for handling the constraint that transfer coefficients must sum to one. An illustrative case study demonstrates the framework under simplified conditions, and the authors state further work is needed before systematic application.

dynamic_shocks.title: A security reclassification abruptly narrows access to Europe’s research ownership and technology transfer
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on research ownership and technology transfer. Separate primary evidence shows that a sudden security reclassification can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of research ownership and technology transfer.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for a sudden security reclassification.
Primary evidence contains 2 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
1 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.

dynamic_shocks.title: A security reclassification abruptly narrows access to Europe’s research talent
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on research talent. Separate primary evidence shows that a sudden security reclassification can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of research talent.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for a sudden security reclassification.
Primary evidence contains 1 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
1 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
2 historical Strand-A item(s) provide structural context; they cannot serve as the current trigger.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on research talent for current or planned work.
A sudden security reclassification reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: Only one primary retained record currently links the European capability directly to the outside pressure.
The primary direct connection is concentrated in one source, so independent confirmation is still weak.
The primary corpus contains 5 strong sign(s) of substitution, resilience or policy response that could absorb the shock.
Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Improve long-term research careers so recruited scientists can stay through a disruption.
Use common European mobility and screening rules instead of many conflicting national responses.
Use common, targeted screening rules rather than broad restrictions that fragment European access.
watch_for: Research previously treated as open is moved into a more restricted security category.
Different European countries apply materially different access decisions to the same work.
dynamic_shocks.net_assessment: Plausible, but important parts of the primary trigger or connection still need confirmation.
